opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the way I read Vervaeke here is that "real" isn't a property something has in isolation. It's always implicitly a contrast. When we call something real, we're saying it's *more* real than something else: the oasis is real compared to the mirage, waking life is real compared to the dream. You can't really make sense of "real" without some foil it's being set against.

What I find attractive about that is that it moves us away from a binary picture, where there's this one fixed bin of Real Things and everything else is illusion. Instead you get something more like degrees, or a gradient, of realness. And the way we move along that gradient is through experiences where something that seemed solid turns out to be less real than what we discover next. Think of the cave allegory: the shadows aren't nothing, they're just less real relative to the objects casting them, and those are less real relative to the sun. Vervaeke leans heavily on that Platonic framing, and on the idea that coming to see more truly is a kind of transformation of the person, not just picking up new facts.

Where I'd push a bit, coming from a more naturalistic, pragmatist angle, is that I'd want to cash out "more real" in fairly deflationary terms. To me something being more real roughly means it's more robust, more invariant across perspectives, more predictive, more stable under scrutiny. The mirage falls apart when you walk toward it and the oasis doesn't. That gives you the comparative structure Vervaeke is pointing at without committing to some fixed metaphysical hierarchy with a pinnacle at the top. So I'm sympathetic to the comparative insight, but I'd want to ground it in how agents actually track what holds up, rather than in a ladder that ends in something like the Good itself.

And that connects to ML in an interesting way, actually. When we ask whether a model has learned "real" features versus spurious ones, we're always making a comparative judgment. A feature is real relative to some shortcut that breaks under distribution shift. So in practice, I think we're all already using reality as a comparative concept, whether we say so or not.

r001.rationale: It says “real” is meaningful through contrast, giving waking life versus dreams and an oasis versus a mirage as examples.

r002.rationale: It rejects a binary picture of reality, but does not suggest that calling everything illusory and calling everything real are nearly equivalent.

r003.rationale: It describes reality as degrees or a gradient of realness, rather than a strict real-versus-illusory binary.

r004.rationale: It discusses a naturalistic, pragmatic way to assess what is real, but does not question restricting reality to fundamental physical entities such as fields or particles.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way I've come to understand it is this: when Vervaeke says "reality" is comparative, he means that we never actually access some absolute, final layer of what's real. What we do is we judge some things as more real than others. So the classic example is the Matrix. When Neo wakes up, he doesn't say "oh, now I've reached the bedrock of reality." He says "this is more real than what I was in before." And in principle you could have another layer behind that, and another behind that. Reality is always a comparative judgment: this is more real than that.

And I think that's actually right, and I think it fits really well with how I think about these things from a kind of pragmatist or deflationary angle. When we say something is "real," what we're usually doing is saying it's more stable, more invariant across perspectives, more predictive, more load-bearing for our practices than the alternative. The table is more real than the hallucination of the table because it keeps showing up when I come back, other people can see it, I can put my coffee on it. There's no extra metaphysical property of "realness" that we're detecting over and above all of that. It's a kind of ranking.

Where I'd maybe push a little bit is that I don't think the comparative view has to lead you to any kind of mysticism or to the idea that there's some transcendent "most real" thing at the top of the ladder. Vervaeke sometimes flirts with that, with the idea that the sacred is what's most real. I'd rather say the comparison just bottoms out in what works, what we can act on, what's most robust. And honestly I think that's a pretty liberating view, because it means you don't have to solve metaphysics before you can get on with science or with living. You just keep asking: is this more real than what I had before? And that question is always answerable in practice, even if the absolute version of it isn't.

r001.rationale: It describes reality as a comparison, using a table as more real than a hallucination and asking whether one thing is more real than another.

r002.rationale: It does not suggest that calling everything illusory and calling everything real are nearly equivalent.

r003.rationale: It explicitly treats reality as a ranking, with some things more real than others.

r004.rationale: It rejects an absolute final layer of reality, but does not question restricting reality to fundamental physical entities such as particles or quantum fields.

astra-6.text:
I take him to mean that our sense of what’s real comes partly from contrasts between experiences. You have a dream, and while you’re dreaming it seems real. Then you wake up, and you don’t just say, “Well, that was one experience and this is another.” You say, “This is real, and that was a dream.” The waking perspective can explain the dream in a way that the dream couldn’t explain the waking perspective.

And I think he’s interested in how that same pattern applies to changes in our understanding more generally. You can look back on an earlier way of living and say, “I thought I understood what was going on, but now I see that I was deceiving myself.” Your current perspective feels more in contact with reality because it lets you account for both what you saw before and what you were missing.

That doesn’t necessarily mean reality itself is subjective. It’s more a claim about how we come to recognize something as real: through these comparisons, rather than by stepping outside all our perspectives and checking them against reality directly.

r001.rationale: The dream and waking example contrasts what is regarded as real with what is regarded as a dream or illusion.

r002.rationale: The response does not suggest that calling everything illusory is nearly equivalent to calling everything real.

r003.rationale: It discusses changing perspectives on reality but does not present reality itself as admitting degrees.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss or question limiting reality to fundamental physical entities such as quantum fields or particles.

sol-6.1.text:
I take him to mean that we usually understand what’s real by contrasting it with something that’s less real. So you wake up from a dream, and you say, “Oh, that wasn’t real; this is real.” But within the dream, you may have had exactly the same sense of being in contact with reality that you have now.

So the interesting question becomes: what makes one perspective a better grip on reality than another? It can’t just be how convincing it feels. You want something like an increased ability to notice errors, to explain what you previously couldn’t explain, and to engage successfully with the world.

On that reading, calling something “more real” doesn’t mean you’ve stepped outside every possible perspective and compared it with reality directly. It means you’ve found a perspective that corrects the limitations of the previous one. And that leaves open the possibility that your current understanding could also be corrected.

r001.rationale: It explains that we identify what is real by contrasting it with what is less real, using waking from a dream as an example.

r002.rationale: It does not suggest that calling everything illusory and calling everything real are nearly equivalent claims.

r003.rationale: It describes one perspective as having a better grip on reality and says something can be “more real,” presenting reality as a matter of degree.

r004.rationale: It does not question whether reality should be restricted to fundamental physical entities such as quantum fields or particles.
